opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most exciting directions we've been exploring, because it flips the usual perspective. Normally we treat a neural network as a tool: you train it on data, then you evaluate it on held-out test data. What we started asking is, what if we treat the trained models themselves as data? If you have a large population of trained networks, what we call a model zoo, you can learn a representation of those weights, essentially a hyper-representation, by training something like an autoencoder that maps the weights into a latent space.

What's fascinating is that this latent space turns out to be very structured. Without ever looking at test data, you can predict properties of a model from its embedding: its accuracy, its generalization gap, even hyperparameters it was trained with, or the epoch it came from. The weights carry an imprint of the training process, and the latent space makes it accessible.

Practically, that matters in a few ways. Imagine model hubs with thousands of networks. Running every model on a benchmark is expensive, and sometimes you don't have access to the original data at all because of privacy or proprietary reasons. If you can look at the weights and say "this one will probably perform well" or "this one looks undertrained or even compromised," that's a very cheap screening step.

And because the representation is generative, you can go the other way too. You can sample from the latent space and decode new weights, which gives you a better initialization or even ready-to-use models, kind of a model-of-models.

There are open challenges, of course. Scaling to really large architectures is hard, weight-space symmetries like permutations have to be handled carefully, and generalizing across very different architectures is still an open problem. But I see it as a first step toward treating the whole population of neural networks on the internet as a dataset we can learn from, and that, I think, has huge potential.

r002.rationale: It mentions a population of trained networks and says generalizing across architectures is an open problem, but does not limit the demonstrated prediction to small networks sharing one architecture and training dataset.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says the embedding can predict a model’s generalization gap.

r004.rationale: It mentions an embedding can reveal the epoch a model came from, but does not describe training progression as visible trajectories through latent space.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've been really excited about in my group. The basic idea is this: a trained neural network is, at the end of the day, just a very large vector of numbers. The weights are the artifact that comes out of training. And the question we asked ourselves was, if you have thousands of these trained models, a population of them, can you learn something about a model just by looking at its weights, without ever running it on test data?

So the way we approach it is to take a model zoo, populations of networks trained on the same task with different seeds, different hyperparameters, different initializations, and then learn a representation of those weights in a latent space. Think of it as an embedding, very much like you'd embed images or text, except the input is the weight tensor of a network. And the self-supervised objectives we use try to make that embedding capture the structure of the weights, not just memorize them.

What we found, and this was honestly surprising to us at the beginning, is that this latent space is quite informative. You can take a model you've never seen, embed it, and from that embedding predict things like its test accuracy, its generalization gap, how far along in training it is, sometimes even which hyperparameters it was trained with. And you can do that reasonably well without a single forward pass on held-out data.

Now, why does that matter? There are a few practical angles. One is model selection and auditing. If you're in a setting where test data is expensive, scarce, or you simply can't share it for privacy reasons, having a way to say "this checkpoint is probably better than that checkpoint" is valuable. Another angle is understanding the loss landscape itself. If models from similar training regimes cluster together in the latent space, that tells you something about the structure of the solutions that gradient descent finds. And then there's the more speculative direction, which is going the other way: sampling from that latent space to generate new weights, so the representation becomes a generative model over neural networks.

I should be clear about the limitations, because I don't want to oversell this. The models in our zoos are, by today's standards, small. The approach relies on having a population of models that are reasonably comparable, same architecture, same task family, and generalizing across architectures or across very different tasks is still an open problem. And there's a permutation symmetry issue: you can swap neurons within a layer and get a functionally identical network with a very different weight vector, so you have to think carefully about how to build in or learn invariance to that.

But I'd say the broader takeaway is that weights are data. We've spent a decade learning representations of images, text, audio. Neural network weights are just another modality, and it turns out they have learnable structure too. That reframing, more than any particular result, is what I find most exciting about it.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a very exciting direction, because we usually think of a neural network as something that takes data as input and makes a prediction. But here, the network itself becomes the input. Can we look at its weights, encode them into a latent representation, and learn something about its behavior—perhaps even predict how well it will perform?

Imagine you have a collection of trained networks and you know their performance. You could learn a representation of those networks, then learn a mapping from that representation to performance. For a new network, you would inspect its weights and estimate its performance without running it on test data.

The important qualification is that you’re learning from previous evaluations. You haven’t removed the need for evidence; you’ve moved it into the process of learning that representation. And the question becomes: how well does that relationship generalize? If the new network was trained differently, or is going to operate on a different data distribution, its weights alone may not tell you everything you need to know.

So I see this as a promising way to assess and select models, especially when evaluating every candidate is expensive. But the really interesting research problem is understanding what that latent space captures, and where we can trust its predictions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a very exciting direction, because we usually assess a neural network by looking at its behavior on data. But the question here is: how much can we learn just by looking at the network itself—at its weights?

If we can encode those weights into a useful latent representation, we could potentially learn relationships between that representation and properties such as accuracy or generalization. For a new network, we could then estimate those properties without running it on a test set.

Of course, the representation has to account for the symmetries of neural networks. Two networks can implement the same function while having very different weight arrangements. And predicting performance without test data doesn’t mean that performance is independent of the data distribution. So I see this as a promising way to characterize and compare models, with the important question being how well those predictions transfer to networks and settings we haven’t seen before.
